about: Warm milk simmered with turmeric, a pinch of black pepper and a little fresh ginger, with a few almonds alongside. Haldi doodh is the golden milk that Punjabi families drink in the evening. A glass has **calcium, vitamin D and B12**, and the pepper helps your body use the turmeric.
steps: Pour the milk into a small pot and add the turmeric, black pepper and ginger. Warm over medium-low heat, stirring now and then, until it is steaming and just starting to bubble at the edges, about 5 minutes.
Strain it into a mug and drink it warm with the almonds on the side.
tip: A teaspoon of honey makes it softer and sweeter.

name: Masala peanuts
inspiredBy: Roadside masala moongfali
about: Raw peanuts toasted in a dry pan until golden, then tossed with a little onion, tomato, lemon and chaat masala. It is the crunchy moongfali masala sold at roadside stalls in Delhi and Lahore. Peanuts bring **niacin, vitamin E and plant protein**.
steps: Toast the peanuts in a dry pan over medium heat, shaking often, until they are golden and smell nutty, about 4 minutes. Let them cool for a minute.
Toss the warm peanuts with the onion, tomato, cilantro, lemon juice, chaat masala and black salt and salt, and eat right away while they are still crunchy.

name: Pomegranate chaat
about: Ruby pomegranate seeds tossed with lemon, chaat masala and a little black pepper. It is a sweet, sour and salty snack, and the seeds bring **vitamin C and fibre**.
steps: Scoop the seeds out of the pomegranate into a bowl.
Toss them with the lemon juice, chaat masala and black salt and black pepper and eat right away.

name: Cucumber with chaat masala
inspiredBy: Street-cart cucumber chaat
about: Cold cucumber spears sprinkled with lemon, chaat masala and a pinch of black salt, the way they are sold from street carts across Punjab and Delhi. It is crisp, sour and salty, and very light. The cucumber brings **water, crunch and a little vitamin K**.
steps: Arrange the cucumber on a plate.
Squeeze over the lemon juice and sprinkle with the chaat masala and black salt. Eat right away.

name: Egg sauce with greens and pan-grilled ripe plantain
inspiredBy: Nigerian egg sauce, with collards folded in and the plantain cooked in very little oil
about: Soft eggs stirred through a thick tomato, onion and pepper sauce with a little collard greens, served with golden slices of ripe plantain. It is savoury and sweet on one plate, and quick when the sauce base is made ahead. The eggs bring protein and **choline**, and the plantain adds potassium and vitamin A.
steps: Make the sauce base up to two days ahead. Warm half the oil in a pan, soften the onion and pepper for 4 minutes, then add the tomato and chili. Cook, stirring now and then, until the tomato has broken down into a thick, jammy sauce, about 8 minutes. Chill it.

On the day, peel the plantain and slice it on an angle into thick coins. Brush a non-stick pan with a little of the remaining oil and cook the plantain over medium heat until deep golden and soft, about 3 minutes on each side. Set it aside.
Add the rest of the oil to the pan and warm the sauce through. Stir in the collards with a splash of water and cook until tender, about 3 minutes.
Beat the eggs with the salt, pour them over the sauce and stir gently until they are softly set and still glossy, about 2 minutes. Serve right away with the plantain.
tip: The sauce base keeps for two days in the fridge, so a double batch covers two mornings. Boiled yam is the other classic partner for egg sauce, and ground crayfish is a traditional addition if you have it. Leave out the chili for a mild version.
ingredients: scotch bonnet or habanero (produce aisle), or another hot red chili

name: Moi moi, steamed black-eyed pea pudding, with avocado and orange
inspiredBy: Nigerian moi moi, steamed in ramekins instead of leaves
about: A soft, savoury pudding of black-eyed peas blended with sweet peppers and onion, with half a boiled egg tucked in the middle, served with creamy avocado and a few orange segments. It makes two portions, and the second is just as good reheated the next morning. The peas bring **iron, folate and fibre**, and the avocado brings vitamin E.
steps: On Saturday night, cover the peas with plenty of cold water and leave them to soak overnight.

On Sunday evening, drain the peas and rub handfuls between your palms under water to loosen the skins. Pour off the skins as they float up and repeat until most are gone. It takes about 10 minutes and gives the pale, smooth moi moi you are after.
Hard-boil the eggs for 8 minutes, then cool, peel and halve them.

Blend the peas with the pepper, tomato, onion, chili, dried shrimp and a splash of water until you have a thick batter that drops off the spoon in a slow ribbon. Stir in the vegetable oil, palm oil and salt.

Ladle the batter into lightly oiled ramekins or foil cups, filling them about three quarters full, and press half an egg into the middle of each. For two portions that is four ramekins. Cover tightly with foil.

Stand the cups on a rack in a wide pot with a finger of simmering water, put the lid on and steam for about 40 minutes, topping up the water if it runs low. It is done when it is firm like set custard and a knife comes out clean. Cool and chill.

On Tuesday morning, reheat two ramekins for 2 minutes in the microwave or 10 minutes in a steamer and serve with the avocado and orange. Keep the other two for Wednesday. Moi moi keeps for three days in the fridge.
tip: Skins-on moi moi is darker, grittier and firmer, so it is worth the ten minutes to rub them off. A spoon of fresh pepper sauce or a little millet pap (ogi) on the side is the traditional partner. Foil cups or a muffin tin work if you do not have ramekins.
ingredients: scotch bonnet or habanero (produce aisle), or another hot red chili

name: Spiced millet koko with yogurt, banana and groundnuts
inspiredBy: Hausa koko, the ginger and clove millet porridge of northern Nigeria and Ghana, with yogurt in the spirit of nono, the fermented milk
about: A thick, creamy millet porridge warmed with fresh ginger, clove and black pepper, topped with a big spoonful of cool yogurt, sliced banana and a crunch of chopped roasted groundnuts. It is gentle, a little sweet and keeps you full all morning. Millet is a whole grain with plenty of **magnesium and fibre**, and the yogurt adds protein and calcium.
steps: The evening before, rinse the millet and leave it to soak in plenty of cold water. This is optional, but it cuts the cooking time nearly in half.

Drain the millet and tip it into a pot with about three times as much fresh water, the grated ginger, clove, black pepper and salt. Bring to a boil, then simmer gently, stirring often so it does not catch.
Cook until the grains have burst and the porridge is thick and creamy, about 15 minutes after soaking, or 25 if you skipped it. Add a splash of water if it gets stiff.
For a smoother, more traditional pap, mash it hard with the back of a spoon or give it a few pulses with a stick blender.

Cook the porridge the evening before and chill it, so breakfast is only a reheat. In the morning, warm one portion with a splash of water and spoon it into a bowl. Top with the cool yogurt, the sliced banana and the chopped groundnuts.
Reheat the second portion the next morning in the same way and add the toppings fresh.
tip: Koko is often eaten with akara or bread. For more kick, add extra ginger. Groundnuts are what West Africans call peanuts.

name: Nigerian-style salad with black-eyed peas, corn and avocado
inspiredBy: Nigerian party salad, with black-eyed peas in place of baked beans and a lime and mustard dressing in place of salad cream
about: A big, crunchy bowl of shredded cabbage, tomato, carrot and sweet corn with seasoned black-eyed peas and ripe avocado, in a tangy lime and mustard dressing. It is cool, filling and needs almost no cooking. The peas bring protein, **iron and fibre**, and the raw vegetables bring vitamin C.
steps: If you are starting from dried peas, soak them overnight, then simmer in unsalted water until tender but not mushy, about 40 minutes. Cook a big batch on Sunday and they keep for four days. Drain well.
While the peas are still warm, toss them with a third of the onion, half the lime juice and the salt so they take on the flavour. Let them cool.
Shred the cabbage very finely, chop the tomato and grate the carrot. Slice the rest of the onion into thin rings.
Whisk the rest of the lime juice with the mustard and oil until creamy.
Toss the peas with the cabbage, tomato, carrot, corn and onion in a big bowl. Top with the avocado and spoon the dressing over just before eating.
tip: Canned sardines or a boiled egg are popular additions in Nigeria. Pack the dressing separately if you take it to work.
ingredients: soaked and boiled until tender (or about three times the dry weight in canned)
kernels cut from the cob, or canned

name: Suya-spiced beef with cucumber and collard slaw and sweet potato
inspiredBy: Hausa suya, the peppery peanut-spiced grilled beef of northern Nigeria, with sweet potato in place of bread
about: Thin strips of beef rubbed with a warm, nutty yaji spice mix of ground groundnuts, paprika, cayenne, ginger, garlic and onion, grilled until the edges char, and served with a crunchy cucumber and collard slaw and soft sweet potato. It is hot, savoury and bright with lime. The beef brings **iron and zinc**, and the sweet potato brings vitamin A.
steps: Put the flank steak in the freezer for 20 minutes so it firms up, then cut it across the grain into very thin strips.
Grind the groundnuts to a coarse powder with the paprika, cayenne, garlic powder, onion powder and ground ginger, in a spice grinder or with a mortar. This is your yaji.
Toss the beef in the oil. Add about two thirds of the yaji, mix well and leave for 15 minutes while you cook the sweet potato.
Boil the sweet potato wedges in salted water until just tender, about 12 minutes, and drain well.

Heat a heavy pan over medium-high heat, or heat the broiler. Cook the beef in a single layer for 2 to 3 minutes on each side, until browned at the edges and just cooked through. Do not crowd the pan or it will steam, and watch the peanut coating, which scorches fast.
Slice the cucumber, collards and onion as thinly as you can, chop the tomato and toss with the lime juice. Let it sit for a few minutes so the collards soften.
Serve the beef on the slaw with the sweet potato and a sprinkle of the remaining yaji.
tip: Slice and season the beef the night before and boil the sweet potato with another meal, and lunch is a 10-minute job. Skewers are lovely if you have them. Use less cayenne for a milder version.
ingredients: flank steak, cut as thin as you can

name: Egusi soup with smoked mackerel and bitter greens, with boiled yam
inspiredBy: Nigerian egusi soup, with collards and mustard greens standing in for bitterleaf or ugwu, and smoked mackerel for smoked fish
about: A thick, nutty soup of ground melon seeds cooked in red palm oil with onion, chili and dried shrimp, loaded with collards and mustard greens and finished with flakes of smoked mackerel, served with soft boiled yam. It makes two portions and reheats well. The mackerel brings **omega-3 and B12**, the melon seeds bring magnesium and zinc, and the collards bring calcium.
steps: Peel the yam, cut it into chunks and boil in salted water until tender, 15 to 20 minutes. Drain.

Warm the palm oil in a wide pot over medium heat. Add the chopped onion and cook for 4 minutes, then stir in the garlic, chili and the ground dried shrimp. Let the shrimp sizzle in the oil for a minute so it loses its raw smell.

Stir in the tomato paste and half a cup of water and bring it to a simmer. Grind the melon seeds to a fine powder (or use pre-ground egusi from an African grocery) and stir them with a few spoonfuls of water to a thick paste. Spoon lumps of it into the pot, cover and cook on low for 8 minutes, until it sets into soft curds.
Pour in about another cup of water for two portions, stir gently and simmer for 8 minutes. It should be a thick soup, not a thin one.
Stir in the collards and mustard greens and cook until tender, 8 to 10 minutes.
Flake in the smoked mackerel and warm it through for 2 minutes. Taste before adding any salt.
Serve with the yam, mashed with a fork if you like. Pack the second portion for tomorrow and loosen it with a splash of water when you reheat it.
tip: Pumpkin leaves (ugwu) or frozen bitterleaf are the traditional greens if you can find them at an African grocery, and the same trip will find ground crayfish, ground egusi and iru. Without them, mustard greens give the bitter edge.
ingredients: scotch bonnet or habanero (produce aisle), or another hot red chili
only if needed, the fish is salty

name: Chicken yassa with steamed millet
inspiredBy: Senegalese yassa poulet, with millet in place of the usual white rice
about: Chicken thighs marinated in lime juice, mustard and a mountain of onions, grilled for char, then simmered in the onions until they melt into a sweet and tangy sauce, over fluffy millet. It makes two portions, and the tangy onions taste even better on the second day. The onions and lime bring **vitamin C**, and the millet adds magnesium and fibre.
steps: The night before or that morning, slice the onions. Set aside a small handful of the sliced onion in the fridge for the top, away from the chicken. Mix the rest with the lime juice, vinegar, mustard, crushed garlic, chili, black pepper and half the salt, add the chicken, turn to coat and leave it in the fridge for at least 30 minutes and no more than 12 hours.

Lift the chicken out of the marinade, keeping the onions, and pat it dry. Broil it on a tray for about 4 minutes on each side, until it is nicely charred at the edges. It does not need to be cooked through.
Warm the oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add the marinated onions and the carrot and cook them, stirring often, until soft, golden and jammy, about 15 minutes.
Nestle the chicken into the onions with a splash of water, cover and simmer gently until it is cooked through and the sauce is thick, about 15 minutes.

Meanwhile, rinse the millet and simmer it in about two and a half times as much salted water, covered, until the water is absorbed and the grains are tender, 15 to 20 minutes. Rest it for 5 minutes, then fluff with a fork.

Serve the chicken and onion sauce over the millet, topped with the raw onion you set aside and the parsley. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. Millet turns stiff in the fridge, so add a splash of water and a squeeze of lime when you reheat it.
tip: Marinate the night before or that morning, since much longer in lime and the chicken goes soft. Dijon mustard is the traditional choice. In Senegal yassa is often served with rice, and fish yassa made with a firm white fish is just as good.
ingredients: scotch bonnet or habanero (produce aisle), or another hot red chili

name: Groundnut stew with beef, sweet potato and collards
inspiredBy: Senegalese mafe and Ghanaian groundnut soup, with collards for the greens
about: Tender beef and soft sweet potato in a thick, savoury groundnut and tomato sauce with ginger, garlic and chili, with collards stirred in at the end and a squeeze of lime to cut the richness. It is rich without needing much oil, and it makes two portions. Groundnuts are a great source of **vitamin E**, and the sweet potato and collards add vitamin A, calcium and vitamin K.
steps: Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat and brown the beef in batches until well coloured on all sides. Set it aside.

Lower the heat and soften the chopped onion with the ginger, garlic and chili for 5 minutes. Stir in the tomato paste for a minute, then the chopped tomato, and cook until it darkens and thickens, about 8 minutes.
Return the beef to the pot with a mug of water and the salt. Cover and simmer gently until the beef is tender, about 60 minutes (or 25 minutes in a pressure cooker).
Add the sweet potato and enough water to nearly cover. Simmer for 12 minutes, until it is soft.

Blend the groundnuts with a ladle of the hot broth until completely smooth, then stir it into the pot along with the collards. Simmer very gently for 10 more minutes, stirring now and then, until the sauce is thick and glossy. Do not let it boil hard or the groundnuts can catch.
Stir in the lime juice and taste for salt. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. The stew thickens in the fridge, so loosen it with a splash of water.
tip: Cassava is the other classic here. Natural peanut butter, stirred in with the broth, is a fine shortcut for the blended groundnuts, and chicken thighs cook in half the time.
ingredients: flank steak, cut in bite-size pieces
scotch bonnet or habanero (produce aisle), or another hot red chili

name: Grilled tilapia with onion and chili sauce, boiled cassava and stewed greens
inspiredBy: Ivorian poisson braisé, grilled fish with an onion, tomato and chili sauce, with cassava in place of attiéké and Sierra Leone-style stewed greens
about: Tilapia fillets rubbed with ginger and garlic and broiled until golden, with a tangy raw onion, tomato and chili sauce, soft boiled cassava and collards and mustard greens stewed with a little palm oil and dried shrimp. It is simple, bold and quick to put together. The fish brings lean protein, B12 and selenium, and the greens bring **calcium and vitamin K**.
steps: Peel the cassava, cut it into chunks and cut out the woody core. Boil in salted water until completely soft, about 20 minutes, then drain.
For the sauce, slice half the onion very thinly and chop the tomato and chili. Toss with the lime juice and a pinch of salt and let it sit while you cook. It should be sharp, juicy and fresh.
Grate the garlic and half the ginger and rub them over the tilapia with the vegetable oil and a pinch of salt. Lay the fillets on a tray lined with oiled foil.
Heat the broiler to high. Broil the fish for about 4 minutes without turning, until it is opaque and flakes easily. Thin fillets cook fast, so watch them.

Meanwhile warm the palm oil in a pan, chop the rest of the onion and soften it with the rest of the ginger and the ground dried shrimp for 3 minutes, letting the shrimp sizzle. Add the collards and mustard greens with a splash of water, cover and cook until tender and glossy, about 8 minutes.
Serve the fish with the cassava, the greens and a big spoonful of the onion sauce.
tip: Boiled yam or plantain are the other classic partners. A whole fish grilled over charcoal is the real thing, and you would need about 450 g for one portion. Leave the chili out of the sauce for a mild version.
ingredients: scotch bonnet or habanero (produce aisle), or another hot red chili

name: Red-red, black-eyed pea stew with pan-fried ripe plantain and egg
inspiredBy: Ghanaian red-red, with the plantain pan-fried in very little oil instead of deep-fried
about: Black-eyed peas simmered until creamy in a deep red palm oil, tomato, onion and ginger sauce, with sweet pan-fried plantain and a boiled egg on the side. It is the classic Ghanaian comfort plate, and it makes two portions. The peas are a great source of **folate, iron and fibre**.
steps: Soak the peas overnight in plenty of cold water. Drain, cover with fresh water and simmer until completely soft, about 45 minutes (or 15 in a pressure cooker). Do not salt them until they are tender. Keep a mug of the cooking water.
Blend the pepper with half the onion and the tomato. Chop the rest of the onion finely.

Warm the palm oil gently in a wide pot, then soften the chopped onion with the ginger, chili and the ground dried shrimp for about 5 minutes. Add the tomato paste and cook for a minute, then the blended tomato mixture.
Cook, stirring, until the sauce turns a deep red and the oil starts to separate, about 12 minutes. This is where the name comes from.
Stir in the drained peas, the salt and a good splash of the cooking water. Simmer for 15 minutes, mashing a few peas against the side of the pot to thicken the stew.

While it simmers, hard-boil the eggs for 8 minutes. Slice the plantain into thick coins, toss with the vegetable oil and a pinch of salt and cook in a non-stick pan over medium heat for about 4 minutes on each side, until caramelized at the edges.

Serve the peas with the plantain, a halved egg and a few slices of avocado. Pack the second portion of stew for tomorrow. At lunch, pan-sear fresh plantain for 8 minutes while you reheat the stew, as plantain is never as good reheated.
tip: Many cooks add a little fried fish on top. A spoonful of gari is the other traditional topping. Two cans of drained black-eyed peas will save you the simmering time.
ingredients: scotch bonnet or habanero (produce aisle), or another hot red chili

name: Thieboudienne-inspired fish and vegetable rice
inspiredBy: Senegalese thieboudienne, with brown rice cooked in the fish and vegetable broth
about: Fish seasoned with a parsley, garlic, chili and lime paste, laid over brown rice cooked in a rich tomato broth with sweet potato and cabbage. It is Senegal's national dish, simplified for a home kitchen, and it makes two portions. The sweet potato and cabbage add **vitamin A and fibre**, and the fish brings lean protein.
steps: Rinse the rice and soak it in cold water for 30 minutes. Brown rice is chewier than the broken rice used in Senegal, so the soak helps.
Make the paste (called rof): crush or blitz the parsley, garlic, half the onion, the chili, half the lime juice and a pinch of salt into a rough paste.
Cut a few slashes in each fish fillet and press about half of the paste into them. Let the fish sit in the fridge while you start the sauce.

Heat half the oil in a large, heavy pot and soften the remaining onion for 5 minutes, along with the ground dried shrimp. Stir in the tomato paste and fry until it darkens to brick red, about 4 minutes. Add the rest of the paste and about 3 cups of water for the two portions, bring to a boil and simmer for 10 minutes.
Add the sweet potato, tomato and cabbage and simmer for 15 minutes, until the sweet potato is tender. Lift the vegetables out onto a plate and keep them warm.

Ladle off all but about 1½ cups of the broth for the two portions and keep it hot to spoon over at the table. Drain the rice and stir it into the broth left in the pot. Cover and cook very gently, stirring once or twice, until the rice is tender and has soaked up the broth, 35 to 40 minutes.

While the rice finishes, warm the rest of the oil in a pan and sear one fillet for 3 minutes on each side. Lay it on the rice with half the vegetables and finish with the rest of the lime juice and some of the hot broth.

Pack the second portion of rice and vegetables for tomorrow's lunch and keep the second fillet raw in the fridge. Tomorrow, sear it fresh for 3 minutes a side while you reheat the rice with a splash of water.
tip: White rice or broken rice gives the soft, broth-soaked texture and the crispy bottom. Snapper or cod work as well as haddock, and mackerel makes a richer pot. Cassava and eggplant are classic additions.
ingredients: scotch bonnet or habanero (produce aisle), or another hot red chili

name: Goat and yam pepper soup with collards
inspiredBy: Nigerian goat pepper soup, a clear, fiery broth with ginger and warm spices, with yam and collards added to make it a meal
about: A clear, peppery goat broth warmed with ginger, garlic, scotch bonnet, black pepper, nutmeg, clove and allspice, with soft chunks of yam and collards added at the end. It is light, spicy and deeply comforting. The goat brings protein, iron and zinc, the collards bring **calcium and vitamin K**, and the yam brings potassium.
steps: Blend the onion, ginger, garlic and chili with a splash of water into a rough paste.

Put the goat in a pot with the paste, black pepper, nutmeg, clove, allspice and salt and cover with water by a few centimetres. Bring to a boil, skim off the foam and simmer gently until the goat is tender, about 60 minutes (or 25 in a pressure cooker), skimming off any fat that rises.
Add the yam and simmer for another 15 minutes, until the yam is tender and the broth has thickened slightly.
Stir in the collards and simmer for 6 minutes, until tender. Squeeze in the lime juice and taste for salt and heat.
Serve very hot, in a big bowl.
tip: The weight is for boneless goat. If you buy it on the bone, as most cooks do, buy about 250 g and take the bones into the pot. Look for goat at a halal butcher or a Caribbean or African market, and use lamb or chicken thighs if you cannot find it. A teaspoon of ready-made pepper soup spice from the African grocery can replace the ground spices, and a few basil leaves stand in for scent leaf. Goat comes in bigger packs, so make a double pot and freeze the second bowl.
ingredients: about ½ scotch bonnet or habanero, or another hot red chili

name: Groundnut and sesame bites
inspiredBy: Hausa kuli-kuli, the crunchy groundnut snack, here with sesame and without the pressing and frying
about: Roasted groundnuts pounded with toasted sesame (benne) seeds, fresh ginger and a little chili into nutty, crumbly little balls with a crunch of sesame. The sesame brings **calcium** and the groundnuts bring vitamin E.
steps: Toast the sesame seeds in a dry pan over medium heat until golden and fragrant, about 2 minutes.
Grind half the groundnuts in a spice grinder or mortar until they turn oily and start to clump. Roughly crush the other half so some pieces stay coarse.
Mix both with the sesame seeds, ginger, chili and salt, squeeze into small balls and press firmly so they hold together. Eat right away or keep for a day.

name: Orange and roasted groundnuts
about: A juicy orange with a handful of roasted groundnuts, the street snack you will find all over Accra and Lagos. Sweet, salty and crunchy. The orange brings **vitamin C** and the groundnuts bring vitamin E.
steps: Peel the orange, break it into segments and eat it with the groundnuts.

name: Orange yogurt with toasted sesame
about: Thick yogurt with juicy orange segments and a spoonful of toasted sesame (benne) seeds. Cool, sweet and crunchy. The yogurt and sesame together bring **calcium and protein**.
steps: Toast the sesame seeds in a dry pan until golden, about 2 minutes.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl, top with the orange segments and scatter the sesame seeds over.

name: Roasted corn with fresh coconut
about: A large cob of corn roasted until charred in spots, eaten with chunks of fresh coconut, the pairing sold from roadside stalls in Ghana and Nigeria. Sweet, smoky and chewy. Corn brings fibre and B vitamins, and the coconut brings **crunch and fibre**.
steps: Roast the cob over a gas flame, on a hot grill or in a dry heavy pan, turning often, for about 10 minutes, until charred in spots. Sprinkle with the salt and eat it with the coconut chunks.

name: Avocado with tomato and lime
about: Half a ripe avocado with chopped tomato, a squeeze of lime and a pinch of salt. It is creamy, juicy and sharp, the way avocado is eaten across Ghana and Nigeria. Avocado brings **vitamin E**, fibre and potassium.
steps: Halve the avocado and chop the tomato. Spoon the tomato over the avocado, squeeze over the lime juice and sprinkle with the salt.

name: Sardines and tomato on warm yam slices
about: Warm slices of boiled yam topped with canned sardines, chopped tomato, a little onion and chili. Canned sardines are a staple pantry food across West Africa. Sardines eaten with their soft bones bring omega-3, **calcium and vitamin D**.
steps: Slice the yam into thick rounds and boil in salted water until tender, about 12 minutes. Drain. If you have leftover boiled yam, just warm it.
Chop the tomato, onion and chili and mix with the lime juice. Top the warm yam with the sardines, broken into chunks, and the tomato mixture.
ingredients: canned in oil, drained, with the soft bones
scotch bonnet or habanero (produce aisle), or another hot red chili

name: Roasted groundnuts
about: A handful of roasted groundnuts, the simplest snack in West Africa, sold in little twists of paper on every corner. Crunchy and satisfying, with protein and plenty of **vitamin E**.
steps: Sprinkle the groundnuts with a pinch of salt if they are unsalted, and eat them as they are.

name: Ripe banana and roasted groundnuts
about: A ripe banana with a handful of roasted groundnuts, a simple, filling pairing sold at roadsides across Ghana. The banana brings **potassium** and the groundnuts bring protein and vitamin E.
steps: Peel the banana and eat it with the groundnuts.

name: Fresh coconut and roasted groundnuts
about: Chunks of fresh coconut with a handful of roasted groundnuts, a roadside favourite in Ghana. Sweet, crunchy and filling. The groundnuts bring protein and **vitamin E**.
steps: Crack the coconut, pry out the flesh and cut it into chunks. Eat it with the groundnuts.

name: Boiled egg with tomato and fresh pepper
about: A hard-boiled egg with juicy tomato, a little thinly sliced onion and chopped chili and salt. Fresh, hot and simple, and a good source of protein and **choline**.
steps: Hard-boil the egg for 8 minutes, then cool and peel it.
Slice the egg and tomato onto a plate, scatter with the onion and chili and sprinkle with the salt.
ingredients: scotch bonnet or habanero (produce aisle), or another hot red chili

name: Akara, black-eyed pea fritters, pan-fried
inspiredBy: Nigerian akara, pan-fried in a little oil instead of deep-fried
about: Little golden fritters of blended black-eyed peas, onion and chili, pan-fried in just a little oil until crisp outside and fluffy inside. Akara is eaten for breakfast and as a snack across Nigeria and Ghana. The peas bring **iron, folate and fibre**.
steps: Soak the peas in plenty of cold water for at least 4 hours, or overnight. Rub them between your palms to loosen the skins and rinse most of them away.
Blend the peas with the onion, chili, salt and just enough cold water to make a thick, fluffy batter. Beat it hard with a spoon for a minute to add air.
Warm the oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat. Drop in spoonfuls of batter and fry for 2 to 3 minutes on each side, until deep golden and crisp. Drain on paper and eat warm.
ingredients: scotch bonnet or habanero (produce aisle), or another hot red chili

name: Japanese breakfast set: tofu and wakame miso soup, tamagoyaki and brown rice
inspiredBy: a classic Japanese asa-gohan breakfast, with brown rice and a walnut furikake on top
about: A proper Japanese morning: miso soup with tofu and wakame, a rolled omelette (tamagoyaki), warm brown rice under a sprinkle of toasted sesame, nori, bonito and walnuts, and a quick cucumber pickle. With rice from your batch it is about 15 minutes. The **eggs bring protein and choline**, and the soup is warm and easy on the stomach.
steps: Reheat a portion of your batch rice with a splash of water, covered, until steaming. A couple of minutes in the microwave is fine.
Slice the cucumber thinly and toss it with a few drops of the tamari and half the sesame seeds. Leave it to soften while you cook.

Bring about 220 ml (a scant cup) of water to a gentle simmer, add the bonito flakes and steep for 2 minutes, then strain them out and squeeze them dry. Add the wakame (a pinch swells into a lot) and the tofu to the broth, and simmer for 2 minutes.
Turn off the heat. Whisk the miso with a ladle of the broth until smooth, then stir it back in. Don't boil it once the miso is in, which keeps the flavour mellow. Sprinkle with half the scallion.

Start the eggs while the dashi steeps. Beat the eggs with the mirin, the rest of the tamari and the rest of the scallion, finely sliced. Warm the oil in a small non-stick pan over medium-low heat, pour in a thin layer of egg, and roll it up when it has just set. Push the roll to one side, pour in more egg under it, and roll again until the egg is used up.

Toast the squeezed bonito flakes in a dry pan with the chopped walnuts and the rest of the sesame seeds until the flakes are dry and crisp, about 2 minutes. Take the pan off the heat and crumble in the nori. Sprinkle over the rice, and serve with the sliced tamagoyaki, the soup and the pickle.
tip: Short on time? Scramble the eggs softly with the mirin and tamari instead of rolling them. Same flavour, half the fuss.

name: Korean banchan breakfast: soy-braised tofu, soybean sprouts, kimchi, fried egg and rice
inspiredBy: Korean dubu-jorim and kongnamul-muchim, set out the way a home breakfast table has a few small side dishes
about: Golden pan-seared tofu in a garlicky soy, gochujang and gochugaru glaze, with sesame soybean sprouts, a little kimchi, a crisp-edged fried egg and brown rice. The tofu and sprouts are made once and last two mornings, so each breakfast takes about 10 minutes. The **tofu and sprouts bring plant protein and folate**.
steps: The evening before, make the banchan for two mornings (cook double the amounts for 2 portions). Cut the tofu into slabs about 1 cm (½ inch) thick and pat them dry. Warm half the canola oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat and sear the tofu until golden, about 3 minutes a side.

Mince the garlic and scallion. Stir most of them into the tamari, gochujang, gochugaru and a splash of water, pour it over the tofu, and simmer, spooning the sauce over, until it is thick and glossy, about 3 minutes.
Boil the soybean sprouts, covered, in a little water for 5 minutes, until they no longer taste raw. Drain, and toss with the rest of the garlic and scallion, the sesame oil and the sesame seeds.
Cool the tofu and the sprouts and keep them in separate containers in the fridge. They keep for 3 days.
In the morning, reheat the rice and barley with a splash of water, and warm the tofu in the microwave or a small pan for a minute.
Fry the egg in the rest of the canola oil until the white is set and crisp at the edges and the yolk is still soft.
Serve the rice with the tofu and its sauce, the sprouts, the egg and the kimchi.
tip: The evening batch takes about 20 minutes once, and you get two quick mornings out of it.
ingredients: calcium-set, check the label for calcium sulfate

name: Dak-juk, Korean chicken and vegetable rice porridge with walnuts
inspiredBy: Korean dak-juk, made from cooked rice and barley, with walnuts on top like hodu-juk
about: A silky, gently savoury porridge of rice and barley with tender chicken, carrot and zucchini, finished with toasted sesame oil, nori, scallion and crunchy walnuts. It is slow weekend comfort food that makes two bowls, so Sunday's breakfast is already done. The **chicken and barley keep you full** for hours, and the walnuts add plant omega-3.
steps: Mince the ginger and garlic, dice the carrot and zucchini, slice the scallion, and cut the chicken into small pieces.
Warm half the sesame oil in a heavy pot over medium heat. Cook the chicken with the ginger and garlic until it turns white, about 3 minutes.
Add the carrot and the cooked rice and barley, and pour in water to cover the grains by about 3 cm (1 inch). That is roughly 3 parts water to 1 part cooked grain.

Bring to a boil, then simmer over low heat, stirring often and pressing some of the grains against the side of the pot, for about 20 minutes. Add water as it thickens, until the porridge is thick and creamy. Stir in the zucchini and tamari for the last 5 minutes.
Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes, then chop them roughly.

Ladle one portion into a bowl and finish with the sesame oil, scallion, walnuts and crumbled nori. Chill the second portion of porridge on its own, and keep its walnuts and nori separate so they stay crisp. Loosen it with a splash of water when you reheat it.
tip: A spoonful of kimchi on the side is very Korean, and wakes the porridge up.

name: Cold soba with chilled tofu and edamame, with a ginger dipping sauce
inspiredBy: Japanese zaru soba, turned into a fuller lunch bowl
about: Chilled buckwheat noodles with cool tofu, edamame and crisp cucumber, dunked in a light, gingery bonito and soy sauce and finished with shredded nori. It is fresh, filling and ready in about 20 minutes. The **tofu and edamame carry the protein**, and the buckwheat gives it a nutty flavour and a little extra fibre.
steps: Make the dipping sauce first so it can chill. Simmer about 60 ml (¼ cup) of water with the bonito flakes, tamari and mirin for 2 minutes, then strain. Stir in the vinegar and half the grated ginger, and cool it quickly in a bowl set over ice, or the night before in the fridge.
Boil the edamame for 3 to 4 minutes, drain and cool them under cold water.

Cook the soba in plenty of boiling water for the time on the package, usually 4 to 5 minutes. Drain, then rinse really well under cold running water, rubbing gently, until the noodles are chilled and no longer slippery.
Pile the noodles on a plate with the tofu, the cucumber cut into matchsticks and the edamame. Scatter over the sesame seeds, the sliced scallion and the nori cut into thin strips with scissors.
Serve with the sauce and the rest of the ginger for dunking.
tip: Stir a little hot noodle water into the leftover sauce and drink it at the end, the Japanese way.
ingredients: calcium-set, check the label for calcium sulfate, chilled, cubed

name: Tofu steak and onigiri bento with broccoli goma-ae and carrot-daikon pickle
inspiredBy: a Japanese bento of onigiri and kohaku namasu, with a soy-glazed tofu steak for the protein
about: Two small rice balls seasoned with bonito flakes and sesame, wrapped in crisp nori, with a sweet-soy tofu steak, broccoli in a sesame dressing and a bright carrot and daikon pickle. It is the lunchbox you can eat cold at your desk. The **tofu brings plant protein**, the broccoli adds vitamin C and folate, and the pickle adds crunch.
steps: The night before, make the tofu, the broccoli and the pickle. Peel the carrot and daikon and cut them into thin matchsticks. Toss with the vinegar and half the mirin, squeeze lightly, and leave to pickle.
In the morning, reheat the rice and barley until steaming hot. The barley makes it sticky enough to shape.

Pat the tofu dry and cut it into two slabs. Sear it in the oil over medium heat until golden, about 3 minutes a side. Add most of the tamari and most of the remaining mirin to the pan and turn the tofu in the sizzling glaze for a minute, until it is sticky and dark.

Cut the broccoli into small florets and boil for 2 minutes, then drain and cool under cold water. Toss with a few drops of the tamari, a drop of the mirin and half the sesame seeds, to make the goma-ae.

Stir the bonito flakes with the last of the tamari until damp, and mix them into the warm rice with the rest of the sesame seeds. Wet your hands and press the rice firmly into 2 triangles or balls, or press it in plastic wrap and twist.
Pack the onigiri with the tofu, broccoli and pickle, and keep the nori separate. Wrap each onigiri in a strip of nori just before eating so it stays crisp.
tip: Everything except the onigiri can be made the night before. Shape the rice in the morning and wrap the balls in plastic wrap.

name: Natto soba with grated daikon, scallion, nori and kimchi, with bok choy ohitashi
inspiredBy: Japanese natto soba, with kimchi for crunch and a simple ohitashi side
about: Cold buckwheat noodles topped with sticky, savoury natto, sharp grated daikon, scallion and nori, with a spoonful of kimchi for crunch and bok choy dressed in soy and sesame on the side. It is a fast, very Japanese lunch if you like natto. **Natto is rich in iron and fibre**, and the bok choy adds calcium.
steps: Simmer about 50 ml (3 tbsp) of water with the bonito flakes, half the tamari and the mirin for 2 minutes, then strain and cool it in the fridge or over ice. This is the noodle sauce.

Boil the bok choy for 1 to 2 minutes, until just tender and still bright green. Drain, cool under cold water, squeeze lightly and cut into chunks. Toss with a few drops of the tamari and the sesame seeds.
Cook the soba in plenty of boiling water for the time on the package, then drain and rinse well under cold running water until chilled.
Grate the daikon and let it drain a little. Stir the natto briskly with chopsticks about 30 times, until it turns pale and stringy, then stir in the rest of the tamari and most of the scallion.

Put the noodles in a bowl and top with the natto, the grated daikon and the kimchi. Crumble the nori over, add the last of the scallion, pour the cold sauce around the noodles, and serve with the bok choy.
tip: Natto keeps well in the freezer, so buy a few packs on your next trip to an Asian grocery. Not a natto fan yet? Stir in extra grated daikon and a splash of vinegar. Both calm the smell and the stickiness.

name: Hot soba in ginger broth with salmon, bok choy and a soft egg
inspiredBy: Japanese hot kake soba and tsukimi soba, with canned salmon as a quick topping
about: Hot buckwheat noodles in a savoury bonito and soy broth with flaked salmon, bok choy, ginger and a soft egg that poaches in the broth. It is a warming Saturday lunch that takes about 20 minutes. The **canned salmon brings omega-3 and vitamin D**, plus calcium from its soft bones.
steps: Simmer about 300 ml (1¼ cups) of water with the bonito flakes for 3 minutes, then strain it back into the pot. Add the tamari, mirin and half the ginger, cut into thin matchsticks, and keep it at a gentle simmer.
Add the bok choy to the broth and simmer for 2 minutes, until the stems are just tender. Add the salmon in chunks. Crack the egg into the broth, cover, and let it poach for 2 minutes.
While the egg poaches, cook the soba in plenty of boiling water for the time on the package. Drain it and rinse briefly so it does not clump.
Put the noodles in a deep bowl and ladle over the broth, salmon, bok choy and egg. Top with the scallion, the rest of the ginger and the crumbled nori.
tip: A shake of shichimi togarashi on top is a good finish, if you have it.

name: Chicken teriyaki with bok choy, carrots and brown rice
inspiredBy: Japanese teriyaki, with mirin and no added sugar in the sauce
about: Juicy pan-seared chicken thigh glazed in a glossy ginger and soy sauce, with tender bok choy, carrots and chewy brown rice and barley. The sauce is just tamari, mirin, ginger and garlic, so it is far less sweet and less salty than the bottled kind. It makes two portions, so tomorrow's **lunch is already packed**.
steps: Stir the tamari, mirin, grated ginger, grated garlic and a splash of water together in a small bowl.

Pat the chicken dry and cut it into broad strips. Warm the oil in a wide non-stick pan over medium-high heat (use two batches if the pan is crowded) and sear the chicken for 2 to 3 minutes a side, until golden. Move it to a plate.
Add the carrot, sliced into thin coins, and a splash of water to the pan, cover and steam for 2 minutes. Add the bok choy and steam 2 minutes more, until the stems are just tender.
Return the chicken to the pan and pour in the sauce. Simmer, stirring, until it turns glossy and clings to the chicken, about 2 minutes. The chicken should be cooked all the way through with no pink.
Reheat the rice and barley. Serve the chicken and vegetables over the rice with a few drops of the vinegar over the bok choy, then the sesame seeds and sliced scallion.
Pack the second portion, rice and all, for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Cold teriyaki chicken is just as good in a bento. Pack some cucumber slices on the side.

name: Miso-glazed salmon with sesame spinach, grilled mushrooms and brown rice
inspiredBy: Japanese miso salmon and spinach gomae
about: A salmon fillet broiled until nearly done, then brushed with a thin miso, mirin and ginger glaze so it caramelizes without scorching, with grilled king oyster mushrooms, spinach in a nutty sesame dressing and brown rice and barley. Salmon brings **omega-3 fats and vitamin D**, and the sesame spinach adds folate and vitamin K.
steps: Heat the broiler to high and line a tray with foil. Stir the miso, mirin and grated ginger together into a thick paste.
Pat the salmon dry and put it on the tray. Toss the mushrooms with the oil and a few drops of the tamari and set them alongside. Broil about 15 cm (6 inches) from the heat for 5 minutes.
Spread the paste thinly over the salmon and broil 3 to 4 minutes more, until the glaze browns in spots and the salmon flakes easily. The mushrooms should be golden and tender.
Meanwhile, boil the spinach for 30 seconds, then drain, rinse under cold water and squeeze it very dry. Cut it into chunks.

Crush the sesame seeds in a mortar, or in a bowl with the back of a spoon, until about half are ground. Stir in the rest of the tamari, the vinegar and a teaspoon of water, then toss the spinach through it.
Reheat the rice and barley. Serve the salmon and mushrooms with the sesame spinach and the rice, with sliced scallion on top.
tip: No broiler? Bake at 220°C (425°F) for 8 minutes, glaze, then 3 to 4 minutes more.

name: Doenjang jjigae with beef, tofu, zucchini and mushrooms, over barley rice
inspiredBy: Korean doenjang jjigae, with a bonito broth in place of dried anchovy
about: A bubbling, savoury Korean stew of thin beef, tofu, zucchini and king oyster mushrooms in a garlicky doenjang broth with a little gochujang and gochugaru, served over barley rice (boribap). It is rustic family food, and it tastes even better the next day. The **tofu and vegetables do most of the work**, with just a little beef for iron and zinc.
steps: Simmer about 350 ml (1½ cups) of water per portion with the bonito flakes for 3 minutes, then strain the broth.
Warm the sesame oil in a medium pot over medium heat. Cook the beef with the minced garlic for 2 minutes, until it has lost its pink colour.
Pour in the broth and bring it to a simmer. Whisk the doenjang with a ladle of the hot broth until smooth, then stir it into the pot with the gochujang and gochugaru.
Add the zucchini and mushrooms, cut into chunky pieces, and simmer for 6 minutes. Add the tofu in big cubes and the scallion cut into lengths, and simmer gently for 3 minutes more.
Taste the broth: it should be savoury and a little earthy, not too salty. Add a splash of water if it is.
Reheat the rice and barley, and serve the stew over or beside it in deep bowls. Pack the second portion, with its rice, for tomorrow's lunch and reheat it gently so the tofu stays tender.
tip: Add an extra spoon of gochujang for a spicier bowl. Barley is about half the grain here, the way Korean boribap is.

name: Salt-grilled mackerel with grated daikon, spinach ohitashi and wakame cucumber
inspiredBy: Japanese saba shioyaki, set out as a teishoku with ohitashi and a vinegared side
about: A mackerel fillet salted and grilled until the skin is crisp and blistered, with a mound of grated daikon and a splash of soy, spinach in a light soy dressing and a sharp wakame and cucumber salad. It is a simple, honest Japanese dinner. Mackerel is one of the best sources of **omega-3 fats**, and the daikon cuts right through its richness.
steps: Sprinkle the mackerel with most of the salt on both sides and leave it for 20 minutes, then pat it dry with paper towel.
Boil the spinach for 30 seconds, then drain, rinse under cold water and squeeze it very dry. Cut it into chunks and toss with a few drops of the tamari and half the sesame seeds.

Slice the cucumber thinly and toss it with a pinch of the salt. After 10 minutes, squeeze out the water. Soak the wakame in cold water for 5 minutes, then drain and squeeze it, and toss both with the vinegar and a few drops of the tamari.
Heat the broiler to high. Broil the mackerel skin side up on a foil-lined tray for 8 to 10 minutes, until the skin is blistered and the flesh is opaque all the way through. No flipping needed.
Grate the daikon and drain it lightly. Reheat the rice and barley. Serve the mackerel with the daikon and the rest of the tamari dribbled over, with the spinach, the salad and the rice.
tip: Open a window and turn on the fan. Grilled mackerel smells like a Japanese izakaya, which is not bad at all.

name: Dubu-kimchi, stir-fried pork and kimchi with seared tofu and rice
inspiredBy: Korean dubu-kimchi, with a little mirin to balance sour kimchi
about: Tender pork, carrot and mushrooms stir-fried with tangy, spicy kimchi, piled beside slabs of golden seared tofu with brown rice and barley. It is fast, punchy and deeply savoury, and a favourite at Korean tables. **Kimchi is already salty and sour**, so the sauce needs very little extra, and the tofu adds plant protein.
steps: Pat the tofu dry and cut it into slabs about 1 cm (½ inch) thick. Warm half the canola oil in a large non-stick pan over medium heat and sear the tofu until golden, about 3 minutes a side. Move it to a plate.
Add the rest of the canola oil to the same pan. Stir-fry the carrot, mushrooms and pork over high heat for 3 minutes, until the pork has lost its pink colour.
Add the garlic and kimchi and stir-fry for 4 to 5 minutes, until the carrot is tender and the kimchi smells toasty and its edges caramelize.
Stir in the tamari, the mirin and a splash of water, and cook 1 minute more. Take it off the heat and stir through the sesame oil.
Reheat the rice and barley. Serve the kimchi and pork beside the warm tofu and the rice, with the scallion and sesame seeds on top.
tip: Older, sour kimchi is best for cooking. Fresh kimchi works too, but add a splash of vinegar.

name: Bibimbap with beef, four namul and a fried egg
inspiredBy: Korean bibimbap, with brown rice and less oil
about: A big bowl of brown rice topped in sections with sesame spinach, soybean sprouts, carrot and shiitake namul, marinated beef and a crisp-edged fried egg, all mixed together with a tangy gochujang sauce. It is the weekend project: lots of small steps, none of them hard, and it makes two portions. The colourful vegetables carry **folate, vitamin A and vitamin K**.
steps: Make the sauce. Stir the gochujang with the vinegar, about a third of the sesame oil, a little of the garlic and a splash of water into a thick, spoonable paste.
Toss the thinly sliced beef with a little tamari, garlic and a few drops of sesame oil, and leave it to marinate while you do the vegetables.

Blanch the spinach for 30 seconds, drain, rinse cold and squeeze dry. Toss it with garlic, a few drops of sesame oil and a few drops of tamari. Boil the soybean sprouts, covered, in a little water for 5 minutes until they no longer taste raw, then drain and season the same way.

Cut the carrot into matchsticks and slice the shiitake. Stir-fry the carrot in a little sesame oil for 2 minutes, then the shiitake for 3 minutes until golden, seasoning each with a few drops of tamari. Keep the vegetables in separate piles.
Cook the beef in a hot pan for 2 minutes, until it is browned and there is no pink left.
In the same pan, with a little more sesame oil, fry an egg, sunny side up, until the white is crisp at the edges and the yolk is still runny.

Reheat the rice and barley with a splash of water. Divide the rice, namul and beef in half. Put one half in a wide bowl, arranged in sections around the edge, with the egg in the middle, a spoonful of the sauce on top and a pinch of sesame seeds. Mix everything together before you eat.
Pack the other half of the rice, namul and beef in a container for tomorrow's lunch, with the sauce on the side. Reheat the beef and rice, and fry a fresh egg then.
tip: Spinach, sprouts, carrot and shiitake can be swapped for any four vegetables you like.

name: Chicken and tofu nabe with napa cabbage and mushrooms, finished with udon
inspiredBy: Japanese mizutaki, finished with udon instead of the usual rice
about: A pot of bonito broth simmered with chicken thigh, tofu, napa cabbage, daikon, king oyster mushrooms and spinach, dipped in a bright soy and mandarin ponzu, then finished with udon noodles and a swirl of egg in the leftover broth. It is a relaxed Sunday supper you can cook right at the table, with **plenty of vegetables in a light broth** and chicken and tofu for protein.
steps: Make the ponzu. Squeeze the mandarin juice into a small bowl and stir in two-thirds of the tamari and the vinegar. Grate a little of the daikon and slice some of the scallion into it, and set it out for dipping.
Simmer about 600 ml (2½ cups) of water with the bonito flakes and the mirin for 3 minutes in a wide, shallow pot, then strain and return the broth to the pot.
Add the chicken, thin rounds of daikon and the white stems of the napa cabbage. Simmer gently for 8 minutes, skimming any foam.
Add the mushrooms (halved lengthwise) and the tofu cubes and simmer for 4 minutes. Add the napa leaves, spinach and scallion for the last minute. The chicken should be cooked through with no pink.
Eat from the pot, dipping everything in the sharp ponzu.

For the finish, add the udon (rinsed under hot water to loosen it) to the remaining broth with the rest of the tamari. Simmer for 2 minutes, then pour in the beaten egg in a slow spiral, cover, and turn off the heat for a minute. Spoon into a bowl with a little scallion.
tip: Any firm white fish works in place of the chicken, and it cooks in about 4 minutes. Fresh or frozen udon is fine too.

calcium-set, check the label for calcium sulfate

name: Warm edamame with sea salt
inspiredBy: Japanese izakaya edamame
about: A bowl of warm shelled edamame with a pinch of salt, the izakaya classic. It is a snack with real staying power. The **edamame bring protein, folate and fibre**.
steps: Boil the edamame for 3 to 4 minutes, or as the package says, then drain well.
Sprinkle with a pinch of salt and eat warm.

name: Mandarin and walnuts
about: A juicy mandarin with a handful of walnuts, the way Jeju mandarins are enjoyed in Korea. It is sweet, crunchy and easy to carry. **Walnuts add plant omega-3 fats**, and the mandarin adds vitamin C.
steps: Peel the mandarin and eat it with the walnuts.

name: Mandarin and toasted almonds
about: A juicy mandarin with a small handful of warm toasted almonds. It is sweet, crunchy and keeps you going. The **almonds bring vitamin E** and calcium, and the mandarin adds vitamin C.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan over medium heat for 3 minutes, until golden and fragrant. Peel the mandarin and eat it with the warm almonds.

name: Mandarin with almonds and walnuts
about: A juicy mandarin with a small handful of almonds and walnuts. It is sweet, crunchy and easy to carry. The **almonds bring vitamin E**, the walnuts bring plant omega-3 fats, and the mandarin adds vitamin C.
steps: Peel the mandarin and eat it with the almonds and walnuts. Toast the nuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes first if you like.

name: Asian pear and walnuts
inspiredBy: Korean fruit and nuts after a meal
about: Cold, crisp, juicy Asian pear slices with a handful of walnuts, a very Korean way to end a meal. It is sweet and crunchy. **Walnuts add plant omega-3 fats** and the pear adds fibre.
steps: Slice the pear and eat it with the walnuts.

name: Asian pear and toasted almonds
inspiredBy: Korean fruit and nuts after a meal
about: Cold, crisp, juicy Asian pear slices with a small handful of warm toasted almonds. It is sweet and crunchy, and a very Korean way to end a meal. The **almonds bring vitamin E**, and the pear adds fibre.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan over medium heat for 3 minutes, until golden and fragrant. Slice the pear and eat it with the warm almonds.

name: Hiyayakko, chilled tofu with ginger and bonito
inspiredBy: Japanese hiyayakko
about: A block of chilled tofu topped with grated ginger, scallion, bonito flakes and a dash of tamari. It is cool, silky and savoury, and takes two minutes. It adds **plant protein and a little calcium**.
steps: Pat the tofu dry and set it on a plate.
Grate the ginger over the top, then add the sliced scallion, bonito flakes and sesame seeds. Dribble with the tamari.

name: Roasted sweet potato (yaki-imo)
inspiredBy: Japanese and Korean street-cart roasted sweet potato
about: A whole sweet potato roasted until the skin crackles and the inside turns jammy and caramelized, the way it is sold from street carts in Japan and Korea in winter. It is naturally sweet with nothing added. It is rich in **vitamin A and fibre**.
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Pierce the sweet potato a few times with a fork, set it on a tray and roast for 45 to 50 minutes, until it feels very soft and some syrup oozes from the skin.
Let it cool for a few minutes and eat it with the skin on.
tip: Roast a whole tray on Sunday and rewarm one in a toaster oven. They keep for 4 days in the fridge.

name: Cucumber and carrot sticks with miso and sesame dip
inspiredBy: Japanese moro-kyu, cucumber with miso
about: Crunchy cucumber and carrot sticks with a savoury miso and sesame dip, a very Japanese snack that is often served with beer or tea. It is light, crisp and low in calories. The carrot adds **vitamin A**, and the dip brings a little sesame for minerals.
steps: Cut the cucumber and carrot into sticks. Stir the miso, mirin, sesame seeds and a few drops of water into a thick dip, and use it for dunking.

name: Soft-boiled egg with toasted nori
inspiredBy: Korean gim and eggs
about: A soft-boiled egg with crisp toasted nori to tear and wrap around bites of the egg. It is a small, savoury snack with a lot of protein. The egg brings **protein and choline**, and the nori adds iodine.
steps: Boil the egg for 6½ minutes, cool it under cold water and peel it. Dribble with a few drops of tamari and eat it with torn pieces of nori.

name: Soy-glazed almonds and walnuts (nut jorim)
inspiredBy: Korean nut jorim (gyeongwa-jorim)
about: Almonds and walnuts toasted in a pan and glazed with a little tamari and mirin until sticky, like the Korean nut jorim side dish. They are savoury, a little sweet and very crunchy. The **almonds bring vitamin E**, and the walnuts bring plant omega-3 fats.
steps: Toast the almonds and walnuts in a dry pan over medium heat for 3 minutes, until they smell nutty.
Add the tamari and mirin and stir for about a minute, until the glaze is sticky and coats the nuts. Cool on a plate so they crisp up.
tip: Make a jar on Sunday. They keep for a week.

name: Korean spicy cucumber salad (oi-muchim)
inspiredBy: Korean oi-muchim
about: Crunchy cucumber in a quick sesame, garlic, vinegar and gochugaru dressing, a Korean side dish you can snack on. It is cool, tangy and a little spicy, and mostly water and crunch, with **almost no calories**.
steps: Slice the cucumber and squeeze it lightly to push out some of the water.
Toss with the sliced scallion, minced garlic, vinegar, gochugaru and sesame seeds, and eat right away.
